I'm always assuming that "heartbeats" or "recursion depth" essentially mean that any proof will eventually either typecheck or "time out". Either way,I assume it will stop running. This is not true in some rare circumstances but I don't have an intuition for when this happens.

I've seen this behavior using aesop and now also with omega:

import Mathlib.Tactic.Basic

theorem false_theorem_omega_is_stuck (s len : UInt64)
    (hlen : len.toNat = 2 * s.toNat)
    (this : (len + s).toNat = (len.toNat + s.toNat) % 2 ^ 64) :
    (len.toNat + s.toNat) % 2 ^ 64 ≠ 0 := by omega

Is this intended?

My problem is that AIs write nonsense theorems and get stuck waiting for omegato fail... Does anyone else have this problem? How do you deal with it?

The problem is that the statement you are trying to prove (len.toNat + s.toNat) % 2 ^ 64 ≠ 0 requires omega to perform modular arithmetic by a huge number 2 ^ 64. The algorithm used by omega is very efficient for small integers, it is not optimized for this scale so it takes a very long time to run. If you replace 2 ^ 64 by a reasonable number you will see that omega immediately finds a counterexample.
Thanks, that's good to know! But is there a way to make omega (and ideally all tactics) reliability fail after "some reasonable" time?

Edit: Yes, see Snir Broshi's comment below.

Unfortunately, no. Tactics in Lean are basically metaprogramming black boxes. They can do anything they want including prompting external AI agents, sending data over the internet, deleting your entire hard drive, etc. (For this reason, you should be extremely careful when running untrusted Lean code)

In this case, omega, aesop and similar tactics implement closed mathematical algorithms. They don't use maxHeartbeats. They don't poll. They don't check the wall clock. They just run until they complete their algorithm and there is no way to interrupt them. The best thing to do is just add a manual system timeout in your terminal like timeout 30s lake build
(it might be possible to simplify the code using TacticM.asTask, not sure)
